readNotes: Pilot batch 2 (Nov 4 2026). Full text read first. Ledger reuse allowed for reader items (Brandon, Nov 4 3:58 PM). Distractors from chapters 0-7 only. Suicide theme handled factually.

w1.text: Siddhartha was deeply shocked. So this was how things were with him, so doomed was he, so much he had lost his way and was forsaken by all knowledge, that he had been able to seek death, that this wish, this wish of a child, had been able to grow in him: to find rest by annihilating his body! What all agony of these recent times, all sobering realizations, all desperation had not brought about, this was brought on by this moment, when the Om entered his consciousness: he became aware of himself in his misery and in his error. Om! he spoke to himself: Om! and again he knew about Brahman, knew about the indestructibility of life, knew about all that is divine, which he had forgotten.

w2.text: Then, out of remote areas of his soul, out of past times of his now weary life, a sound stirred up. It was a word, a syllable, which he, without thinking, with a slurred voice, spoke to himself, the old word which is the beginning and the end of all prayers of the Brahmins, the holy Om, which roughly means "that what is perfect" or "the completion." And in the moment when the sound of Om touched Siddhartha's ear, his dormant spirit suddenly woke up and realized the foolishness of his actions.

w3.text: Deep was his sleep and without dreams, for a long time he had not known such a sleep any more. When he woke up after many hours, he felt as if ten years had passed, he heard the water quietly flowing, did not know where he was and who had brought him here, opened his eyes, saw with astonishment that there were trees and the sky above him, and he remembered where he was and how he got here. But it took him a long while for this, and the past seemed to him as if it had been covered by a veil, infinitely distant, infinitely far away, infinitely meaningless.

w4.text: He observed the man, who had neither hair on his head nor a beard, and he had not observed him for long when he recognised this monk as Govinda, the friend of his youth, Govinda who had taken his refuge with the exalted Buddha. Govinda had aged, he too, but still his face bore the same features, expressed zeal, faithfulness, searching, timidness. But when Govinda, sensing his gaze, opened his eyes and looked at him, Siddhartha saw that Govinda did not recognise him. Govinda was happy to find him awake; apparently, he had been sitting here for a long time and been waiting for him to wake up, though he did not know him.

w5.text: "I believe you, my dear Govinda. But now, today, you've met a pilgrim just like this, wearing such shoes, such a garment. Remember, my dear: Not eternal is the world of appearances, not eternal, anything but eternal are our garments and the style of our hair, and our hair and bodies themselves. I'm wearing a rich man's clothes, you've seen this quite right. I'm wearing them, because I have been a rich man, and I'm wearing my hair like the worldly and lustful people, for I have been one of them."

w6.text: With a smiling face, Siddhartha watched the leaving monk. The sleep had strengthened him much, but hunger gave him much pain, for by now he had not eaten for two days, and the times were long past when he had been tough against hunger. With sadness, and yet also with a smile, he thought of that time. In those days, so he remembered, he had boasted of three things to Kamala, had been able to do three noble and undefeatable feats: fasting—waiting—thinking. These had been his possession, his power and strength, his solid staff; in the busy, laborious years of his youth, he had learned these three feats, nothing else. And now, they had abandoned him, none of them was his any more, neither fasting, nor waiting, nor thinking.

w7.text: Now, he thought, since all these most easily perishing things have slipped from me again, now I'm standing here under the sun again just as I have been standing here a little child, nothing is mine, I have no abilities, there is nothing I could bring about, I have learned nothing. How wondrous is this! Now, that I'm no longer young, that my hair is already half gray, that my strength is fading, now I'm starting again at the beginning and as a child! Again, he had to smile. Yes, his fate had been strange! Things were going downhill with him, and now he was again facing the world void and naked and stupid. But he could not feel sad about this, no, he even felt a great urge to laugh, to laugh about himself, to laugh about this strange, foolish world.

w8.text: "Things are going downhill with you!" he said to himself, and laughed about it, and as he was saying it, he happened to glance at the river, and he also saw the river going downhill, always moving on downhill, and singing and being happy through it all. He liked this well, kindly he smiled at the river. Was this not the river in which he had intended to drown himself, in past times, a hundred years ago, or had he dreamed this?

w9.text: Wherever from, he asked his heart, where from did you get this happiness? Might it come from that long, good sleep, which has done me so good? Or from the word Om, which I said? Or from the fact that I have escaped, that I have completely fled, that I am finally free again and am standing like a child under the sky? Oh how good is it to have fled, to have become free! How clean and beautiful is the air here, how good to breathe!

w10.text: "It is good," he thought, "to get a taste of everything for oneself, which one needs to know. That lust for the world and riches do not belong to the good things, I have already learned as a child. I have known it for a long time, but I have experienced only now. And now I know it, don't just know it in my memory, but in my eyes, in my heart, in my stomach. Good for me, to know this!"

w11.text: Now Siddhartha also got some idea of why he had fought this self in vain as a Brahmin, as a penitent. Too much knowledge had held him back, too many holy verses, too many sacrificial rules, to much self-castigation, so much doing and striving for that goal! Full of arrogance, he had been, always the smartest, always working the most, always one step ahead of all others, always the knowing and spiritual one, always the priest or wise one. Into being a priest, into this arrogance, into this spirituality, his self had retreated, there it sat firmly and grew, while he thought he would kill it by fasting and penance.

w12.text: Cheerfully, he looked into the rushing river, never before he had like a water so well as this one, never before he had perceived the voice and the parable of the moving water thus strongly and beautifully. It seemed to him as if the river had something special to tell him, something he did not know yet, which was still awaiting him. In this river, Siddhartha had intended to drown himself, in it the old, tired, desperate Siddhartha had drowned today. But the new Siddhartha felt a deep love for this rushing water, and decided for himself, not to leave it very soon.

w13.text: Quietly, he spoke the word Om to himself, speaking which he had fallen asleep, and it seemed to him as if his entire long sleep had been nothing but a long meditative recitation of Om, a thinking of Om, a submergence and complete entering into Om, into the nameless, the perfected.

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha forgets the word Om forever after that night.
Siddhartha hears a ferryman call to him and swims across.
Siddhartha prays to the gods for help.
Hearing the word Om wakes Siddhartha from his despair.
A.explanation: When "the sound of Om touched Siddhartha's ear, his dormant spirit suddenly woke up and realized the foolishness of his actions." No ferryman calls here. He remembers Om rather than forgetting it. He speaks the word "without thinking," not as a planned prayer to the gods.

A.prompt: According to the passage, how did Siddhartha feel when he woke up?
options: Sick, weak and frightened
Hungry and angry at himself
As if he had slept only a few minutes
As if ten years had passed
A.explanation: The passage says "he felt as if ten years had passed." A few minutes reverses this, and he is by the river, not in the city. Sickness and fear are not described; he wakes to trees and sky. Hunger comes later and anger is not mentioned.

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "dormant" most nearly means
options: wide awake
angry
dead
sleeping
A.explanation: "His dormant spirit suddenly woke up," so dormant means sleeping or inactive. "Wide awake" is what it becomes, not what it was. "Dead" goes too far, since it can wake. "Angry" has no support in the passage. The word describes the part of him that had been asleep and now wakes at Om.

A.prompt: Govinda's behaviour suggests that he is
options: lost in the forest and afraid
searching for Siddhartha
kind and caring even toward a stranger
suspicious of the sleeping man and ready to call others
A.explanation: He sat "for a long time" waiting for the stranger to wake, though "he did not know him," showing care. Nothing suggests suspicion. He is on a pilgrimage, not lost. He does not know the man is Siddhartha, so he is not looking for him.

A.prompt: What has become of the three feats Siddhartha once boasted of?
options: He has lost all three.
He has lost only his fasting.
He has taught them to Govinda.
He has mastered them better than ever.
A.explanation: The passage says "now, they had abandoned him, none of them was his any more, neither fasting, nor waiting, nor thinking." "Mastered them better than ever" reverses this. Govinda is not taught anything. "Neither... nor... nor" shows all three are lost, not only fasting.

A.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "And now, they had abandoned him, none of them was his any more"
"These had been his possession, his power and strength, his solid staff"
"With sadness, and yet also with a smile, he thought of that time."
"In those days, so he remembered, he had boasted of three things to Kamala"
A.explanation: Only "they had abandoned him, none of them was his any more" says what became of the feats. The "boasted of three things" line recalls the past. "These had been his possession" describes what they once were. "With sadness... he thought" shows his mood, not their loss.

A.prompt: The detail of the river "always moving on downhill, and singing" mainly serves to
options: describe a waterfall in the forest
mirror Siddhartha's own downhill fate, met with joy
show that he is tired of walking
show that the river is dangerous and he should leave
A.explanation: He says "Things are going downhill with you!" then sees the river "going downhill... singing and being happy," mirroring his fate with joy. No danger is stressed; he "smiled at the river." No waterfall is named. The detail is about mood, not tiredness.

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha is ashamed and returns to the city to win back his riches.
Siddhartha finds himself starting over like a child and laughs at it.
Siddhartha feels young and strong again.
Siddhartha remembers all he learned as a Brahmin.
A.explanation: He is "starting again at the beginning and as a child," and he "felt a great urge to laugh." He does not plan to return for riches. His "strength is fading" and his hair is "half gray." He says "I have learned nothing," so he does not recall all his learning.

A.prompt: According to Siddhartha, why is he wearing a rich man's clothes?
options: Because he has been a rich man
Because Govinda gave them to him
Because he is going to a wedding
Because he stole them from a merchant
A.explanation: He says, "I'm wearing them, because I have been a rich man." Theft is never mentioned. Govinda remarks on the clothes but did not give them. No wedding is mentioned; he says he is on a pilgrimage. He answers Govinda plainly, explaining his fine clothes by his past as a rich man.

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "parable" most nearly means
options: a boat
a prayer
a story or image that teaches a lesson
a loud noise made by rushing water
A.explanation: He perceives "the voice and the parable of the moving water," and the river seems to have "something special to tell him," so a parable is something that teaches. The noise of water is its "voice," not its parable. A boat and a prayer do not fit.

A.prompt: Siddhartha's thoughts suggest that he believes
options: that his childhood lessons were enough without living them
that he knows nothing at all
experience teaches more deeply than memory alone
that riches are good for him
A.explanation: He knew it long ago but has "experienced only now," and now knows it "in my eyes, in my heart, in my stomach." Childhood knowledge was not enough. He says riches "do not belong to the good things." He clearly knows something now.

A.prompt: The phrase "this wish of a child" suggests that Siddhartha now sees his wish as
options: a childhood game
foolish and immature
innocent and sweet
wise beyond his years
A.explanation: He is "deeply shocked" and calls it "this wish of a child," so he now judges it foolish and immature. "Innocent and sweet" misses the shock and the word "error." "Wise beyond his years" reverses his judgment. "A childhood game" takes "child" literally; the phrase describes his recent wish, not his boyhood.

B.prompt: According to the passage, what held Siddhartha back as a Brahmin and a penitent?
options: His father's anger and strict rules
Too much knowledge, too many verses and rules
Too little effort in his fasting and his studies
Kamala's love
B.explanation: The passage says "Too much knowledge had held him back, too many holy verses, too many sacrificial rules." It says he was "always working the most," so too little effort is wrong. His father's anger and Kamala's love are not named as causes here.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "arrogance" most nearly means
options: fear
modesty
knowledge
pride
B.explanation: "Full of arrogance, he had been, always the smartest... always one step ahead," so arrogance means pride. Modesty is its opposite. "Fear" is not described. "Knowledge" is what fed his pride, but the word names the attitude, not the learning.

B.prompt: Siddhartha's words suggest that his clothes
options: reflect his past rather than what he is now
prove that he is still a rich man in the city
show that he is still a Samana
are borrowed from his friend Govinda
B.explanation: He says "Not eternal is the world of appearances" and that he wears the clothes because "I have been a rich man," so they reflect his past. "Have been" shows he is no longer rich. Nothing says they are borrowed. Govinda notes that his hair is not a Samana's.

B.prompt: What does Siddhartha most celebrate in the passage?
options: Having become the richest man in the city
Having learned to fast
Having found Govinda again
Having escaped and become free
B.explanation: He exclaims "Oh how good is it to have fled, to have become free!" Riches are what he fled. Govinda is not mentioned. Fasting is not mentioned in this passage; he celebrates freedom and fresh air. His joy comes from having left the city behind and being free again.

B.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "Might it come from that long, good sleep, which has done me so good?"
"Wherever from, he asked his heart, where from did you get this happiness?"
"Or from the word Om, which I said?"
"Oh how good is it to have fled, to have become free!"
B.explanation: Only "how good is it to have fled, to have become free" states what he celebrates. The sleep and Om lines are possible sources he wonders about, not his celebration. "Where from did you get this happiness?" asks a question without answering it.

B.prompt: The repetition of "infinitely" at the end of the passage mainly serves to
options: give the exact time he woke beside the river
introduce Govinda as a character
show how distant his past life now seems to him
name the place where he slept
B.explanation: His past seemed "covered by a veil, infinitely distant, infinitely far away, infinitely meaningless," and the repeated word stresses how remote it now feels. No exact time is given; he only "felt as if ten years had passed." Govinda does not appear here. The place is "trees and the sky above him," named outside this phrase.

B.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha builds a boat to cross the river.
Siddhartha meets the ferryman and asks for work.
Siddhartha feels the river has something to teach him and decides to stay near it.
Siddhartha fears the river where he nearly drowned and hurries away from it.
B.explanation: He feels the river "had something special to tell him" and decides "not to leave it very soon." He feels "deep love" for it, not fear. No boat is built. The ferryman does not appear in this passage. He feels drawn to the river and decides to stay beside it to learn from it.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "wondrous" most nearly means
options: frightening
amazing
dull and ordinary
sad
B.explanation: "How wondrous is this!" expresses his surprise at starting over like a child, so it means amazing. "Dull and ordinary" reverses his surprise. He wants "to laugh," so "frightening" and "sad" do not fit. The word describes how amazing the ordinary morning now seems to him after his sleep.

B.prompt: The dashes in "fasting—waiting—thinking" mainly serve to
options: show a pause in his speech
link the three feats to Kamala
set each of the three feats apart for emphasis
show that he has forgotten the order of his feats
B.explanation: Dashes separate and stress each feat, his "possession, his power and strength." They do not show forgetting. Kamala is the listener in the memory, not linked by the dashes. No one is speaking aloud here. The dashes mark each feat separately, stressing how completely he has lost all three.

B.prompt: The passage suggests that, as he speaks Om, Siddhartha
options: recovers knowledge he had forgotten
feels ashamed of being a Brahmin
forgets all he knew of Brahman
decides to leave the river right away
B.explanation: "Om! he spoke to himself... and again he knew about Brahman... which he had forgotten," so he recovers lost knowledge. He does not forget Brahman; he remembers it. Nothing shows shame at being a Brahmin; Om is the Brahmins' holy word. He does not leave the river; he soon sleeps beneath the coconut tree.

B.prompt: The passage is presented mainly as
options: Siddhartha's own reflections, partly in his own words
a conversation between Siddhartha and Govinda by the river
the narrator's summary of Siddhartha's childhood
a story told by the ferryman
B.explanation: "Now, he thought" introduces his own words, and the narrator continues his reflections, so they are his thoughts. Govinda has left. The ferryman does not appear. The passage concerns his present, not a summary of childhood. The passage gives his own reflections, sometimes in direct speech to himself by the river.

B.prompt: How does Passage 2 follow from the moment in Passage 1?
options: He returns to the city.
The awakening brought by Om leads to a deep, renewing sleep.
The sound of Om frightens him so that he cannot sleep.
He wanders back into the forest.
B.explanation: In Passage 1 Om wakes his spirit; in Passage 2 he sleeps deeply "without dreams" and wakes changed. He does sleep. He does not wander into the forest. He wakes by the river, not in the city. The second passage shows Om bringing him rest and renewal instead of death.

C.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: His self was killed long ago by all his fasting and penance among the Samanas in the forest.
His self had hidden inside his pride in being spiritual, which is why fasting failed.
He never once tried to fight against his self.
His teachers were far too strict with him.
C.explanation: "Into this arrogance, into this spirituality, his self had retreated, there it sat firmly and grew, while he thought he would kill it by fasting." Fasting did not kill it. He "fought this self in vain," so he tried. Strict teachers are not named as the reason.

C.prompt: Siddhartha's laughter at his own downhill path suggests
options: acceptance of his fate rather than despair
that he is mocking Govinda for not recognising him at first
that he plans to go uphill
that he has lost his mind
C.explanation: He "laughed about it" and smiled at the river, suggesting acceptance. Govinda is gone and not mocked here. Nothing suggests madness; he reflects calmly. He is glad the river goes "downhill," not planning to climb. He laughs at his fall because he now accepts it as part of his path.

C.prompt: The contrast between "I have known it" and "I have experienced only now" mainly serves to
options: show that he has forgotten the lessons of his childhood
compare himself with his friend Govinda
distinguish knowing about something from living it
praise the riches he gained
C.explanation: He knew long ago that lust and riches are not good, but only now experienced it, distinguishing knowing from living. He has not forgotten it. Govinda is not compared. He says riches "do not belong to the good things." The contrast shows that real knowledge comes only from living through an experience oneself, not from hearing about it.

C.prompt: What does the passage reveal about the two men's recognition of each other?
options: Siddhartha knows Govinda, but Govinda does not know him.
Both men recognise each other at once and embrace like brothers.
Neither man recognises the other at all.
Govinda recognises Siddhartha first.
C.explanation: Siddhartha "recognised this monk as Govinda," but "Govinda did not recognise him." They do not both recognise each other. Siddhartha does know him. Govinda, not Siddhartha, is the one who fails. Govinda's failure to recognise his friend sets up the gentle irony of their meeting by the river.

C.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "Govinda was happy to find him awake"
"He observed the man, who had neither hair on his head nor a beard"
"Govinda had aged, he too, but still his face bore the same features"
"Siddhartha saw that Govinda did not recognise him."
C.explanation: Only "Govinda did not recognise him" gives Govinda's failure to know him. "Govinda had aged" describes his looks. "Happy to find him awake" shows care, not recognition. "He observed the man" describes looking, not who knew whom. The chosen line shows directly that Govinda does not know who Siddhartha is.

C.prompt: As used in the passage, "submergence" most nearly means
options: rising
a serious mistake
silence
complete immersion
C.explanation: His sleep was "a submergence and complete entering into Om," so it means complete immersion. Rising out of water is the opposite. "Silence" and "a serious mistake" do not match "complete entering into." The word describes his long sleep as a deep sinking into Om, "the nameless, the perfected."

C.prompt: The statement that the river "had something special to tell him" mainly suggests that
options: he hears real words in the water
the river is a person in disguise who will speak to him
he is only dreaming
the river seems to him like a teacher with a message
C.explanation: Giving the river "something special to tell him" treats it as a teacher, linked to "the parable of the moving water." It is a feeling ("It seemed to him"), not a person in disguise. No words are heard. He is awake and cheerful.

C.prompt: The passage suggests that, having lost his feats, Siddhartha has become
options: a merchant like Kamaswami
a man stripped of the powers he once relied on
Kamala's servant
a greater Samana than he ever was in the forest
C.explanation: His three feats "had been his possession, his power and strength, his solid staff," and now "they had abandoned him," so he has lost the powers he relied on. Having lost them, he is no greater Samana. He is nobody's servant, and nothing makes him a merchant like Kamaswami; he is alone and hungry.

C.prompt: The series of exclamations beginning "How clean and beautiful is the air" mainly serves to
options: describe the weather in the city he has left behind
warn others away from the forest
convey a rush of joy at being free
show regret
C.explanation: The exclamations celebrate fresh air after fleeing, conveying joy. The city, with its perfumes and wine, was the opposite. No warning is given. He shows delight, not regret. Each exclamation shows how fresh and new the world feels to him now that he is free of the city.

C.prompt: Siddhartha's remark "Not eternal is the world of appearances" mainly serves to
options: insult Govinda for wearing the yellow robe of a monk
ask Govinda for money
explain his changed appearance as part of a larger truth
describe the weather
C.explanation: He uses a general truth to explain why clothes and hair change, making his appearance part of a larger idea. He does not insult Govinda's robe. No weather is described. He asks for nothing. He presents the change in his clothes and hair as an example of the impermanence of all appearances.

C.prompt: How does Passage 2 develop the moment described in Passage 1?
options: It shows him shocked at his error and remembering what he had forgotten.
It shows him deciding at once to return to the city and to his old life.
It shows Govinda arriving to comfort him.
It shows him forgetting the word Om again.
C.explanation: In Passage 1 Om wakes his spirit to "the foolishness of his actions"; Passage 2 shows him "deeply shocked," aware "of himself in his misery and in his error," and again knowing what "he had forgotten." He does not return to the city. Govinda does not appear here. He repeats "Om!" rather than forgetting it.

C.prompt: How does Passage 2 reinterpret the loss described in Passage 1?
options: It ignores the loss entirely.
It suggests that losing those feats freed him from the pride they fed.
It blames Kamala for the loss of his feats.
It suggests the feats were the only path to salvation and must be regained.
C.explanation: Passage 1 mourns losing fasting, waiting and thinking; Passage 2 says his self hid in spiritual pride he fed "by fasting and penance," so the loss freed him. The feats were not the path. Kamala is not blamed. Passage 2 explains rather than ignores the change.
